enum HxMessageDelivery_t

HxMessage Delivery.

These constants define how the messages are delivered: synchronously, or asynchronously. Asynchronous message handling requires that an eventloop be running. Synchronous message handling does not require an eventloop, however the message callbacks are triggered in the context of the underlying thread. This control is used with IPC and timer message handling.

Enumerator:
kHxAsyncMessageDelivery  Messages are delivered asynchronously
kHxSyncMessageDelivery  Messages are delivered synchronously

HxResult HxMessageGetData ( const HxMessage_t *  pMessage,
void **  pData,
unsigned int *  pSize 
)

Get the message data.

This function gets the message data from inside the message instance. If the structure is known then you could typecast or copy the data to the structure, otherwise you have the size field that specifis how many big the data is.

Note that HxSendMessage sends a pointer to the data, while HxPostMessage will have a copied instance of the data. In the case of broadcasted data across processes, then the data is shared in the shared memory and after each process has received the message, the shared memory data is freed.

Parameters:
pMessage IN: Valid message
pData OUT: Handle to the data
size OUT: Size of the data.
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful.

HxResult HxMessagePost ( const HxMessageBroadcaster_t *  pBroadcaster,
HxMessage_t *  pMessage,
HxMessageSenderID_t  senderID 
)

Post a message asynchronously.

This function posts a message asynchronously. If the message has an internal range, the message is queued and any callbacks are triggered later in the context of the process's default user interface thread. This is useful in situations where the receiver must be called in the context of the process's default user interface thread to ensure that data is not accessed by more than one thread in the process. This function should not be used for messages with an external range. For external messages, the thread in which the callbacks are triggered is determined by each individual receiver through HxMessageSetIPCDelivery. The sender has no control over which thread the callbacks are called from. A call to HxMessagePost for an external message will automatically be converted into a call to HxMessageSend.

Parameters:
pBroadcaster IN: Valid broadcaster or NULL for default broadcaster
pMessage IN: Valid message
senderID IN: Sender ID
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful.

HxResult HxMessageRegisterUserMessage ( const char *  messageName,
HxMessageID_t *  id 
)

Register a user message dynamically.

This function registers a new message. The passed in message name should be a unique string, for example consisting of a reverse registered web domain in combination with additional string information. There's no upper limit to the size of the string passed in. You can register the same string mulitple times, getting the same messageID for each registration.

Parameters:
messageName IN: Unique message name
id OUT: Message ID
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful. Returns HX_ALREADY_REGISTERED if the string has already been registered as a message. There's a limit of max user message IDs, if this max limit has been reached, HX_MAX_LIMIT_REACHED is returned.

HxResult HxMessageRemoveCallback ( const HxMessageListener_t *  pListener,
const HxMessageClass_t  messageClass,
const HxMessageID_t  id,
const HxMessageCallback  callback,
const HxMessageSenderID_t  senderID 
)

Remove a specific Message Listener callback.

This function will remove a specific callback that was originally installed for listening to messages. This will free up the resources. It is the responsibility of the client to free any data associated with the callback.

Use sender ID of 0 in case you are not removing a callback targeted to a specific senderID used by ListenToMessageFrom(). Otherwise specify the senderID used in this function.

Note that all callbacks with the same address are removed from the listeners, in other words if you installed the same callback listener multiple times listening for a specific message class and ID, all these callback nodes will be removed.

If the message ID is 0, then the callback is removed from any message ID it has been been installed to. Note that passing a message ID of 0 is slow and inefficient as every installed callback in the process must be checked. Therefore, the use of a 0 message ID is discouraged. If the message ID(s) associated with a callback are known, it is much more efficient to pass the message ID(s) rather than use a 0.

Parameters:
pListener IN: Valid listener
messageclass IN: Message class
id IN: Message ID or 0 in case any ID is valid.
callback IN: Message callback
senderID IN: Message sender ID
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful. Returns HX_NOT_FOUND if the callback was never installed in the first place. Returns HX_NOT_FOUND if the message ID was never used. Returns HX_NOT_FOUND if the callback was already removed.

HxResult HxMessageSend ( const HxMessageBroadcaster_t *  pBroadcaster,
HxMessage_t *  pMessage,
HxMessageSenderID_t  senderID 
)

Send a message synchronously.

This function sends a message synchronously. If the message has an internal range, any callbacks are triggered immediately in the context of the calling thread. Therefore, HxMessageSend should only be used for internal messages if the receiver can safely be called from the same thread as the sender. Note that HxMessagePost should generally be used if the sender is not running in the context of the default user interface thread as any receiver who accesses user interface elements must be called in the context of the default user interface thread. If the message has an external range, HxMessageSend should always be used. In fact, a call to HxMessagePost for an external message will automatically be converted into a call to HxMessageSend. Using HxMessageSend for external messages ensures that the IPC mechanism is immediately triggered. The thread in which any callbacks are triggered is determined by each individual receiver through HxMessageSetIPCDelivery. The sender has no control over which thread the callbacks are called from.

Parameters:
pBroadcaster IN: Valid broadcaster or NULL for default broadcaster
pMessage IN: Valid message
senderID IN: Sender ID
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful.

HxResult HxMessageSetData ( HxMessage_t *  pMessage,
void *  pData,
unsigned int  size 
)

Set the message data.

This function sets the message data fields inside the message instance. Note that the data is not copied when using HxSendMessage, but is copied when using HxPostMessage. In the case of IPC messages, the data is copied into a shared memory segment and each receiver will get access to this shared memory segment that is then freed when the last receiver has received the message.

It is the responsibility of the client to manage and free the actual data.

Parameters:
pMessage IN: Valid message
pData IN: Pointer to the data
size IN: Size of the data.
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful. If size is bigger than the property kHxPropertyMessageMaxDataSize, then HX_RESOURCE_TOO_BIG is returned.

HxResult HxMessageSetIPCDelivery ( HxMessageListener_t *  pListener,
HxMessageDelivery_t  system 
)

Sets the IPC Message delivery system.

This function defines the delivery system the listener will use for delivering IPC messages. There are two kinds, asynchronous (default), and synchronous delivery. The asynchronous delivery will deliver incoming IPC messages asynchronously. This requires an event loop to run in the system. Asynchronous messages handling makes it possible to handle incoming IPC messages inside the gui thread or any other thread running the event loop. Synchronous IPC messaging will immediately trigger message callbacks. There's no need for an event loop to run. However, the message callbacks trigger in the same thread as the underlying IPC messaging implementation. Note that you cannot change the IPC Message delivery system of the default listener. The default listener will always deliver IPC Messages asynchronously.

Parameters:
pListener IN: Valid listener.
system IN: Message delivery system.
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful.

HxResult HxTimerRemoveMessage ( HxMessage_t *  pMessage  ) 

Delete a Timer Message.

Remove a timer message that is queued in the timer. It is the responsibility of the caller to free the memory of the actual message.

Note that any recurring timer messages are removed. Non-recurring timer messages only trigger once and after this they are automatically removed.

Parameters:
IN,: Valid timer message
Returns:
HXResult Returns HX_OK if successful. Returns HX_MISSING_RESOURCE if the timer has already been removed, or if a non-recurring timer has already triggered and removed itself.

HxResult HxTimerSetDelivery ( HxMessageListener_t *  pListener,
HxMessageDelivery_t  system 
)

Sets the Timer delivery system.

This function defines the delivery system the listener will use for delivering timer messages. There are two kinds, asynchronous (default), and synchronous delivery. The asynchronous delivery will deliver timer messages asynchronously. This is the default behavior. It assumes there is an event loop running. Asynchronous messages handling makes it possible to handle incoming timer messages inside the gui thread or any other thread running the event loop. Synchronous timer messaging will trigger message callbacks immediately. There's no need for an event loop to run. However, the message callbacks trigger in the same thread as the underlying timer scheduler. Note that you cannot change the Timer Message delivery system of the default listener. The default listener will always deliver Timer Messages asynchronously.

Parameters:
pListener IN: Valid listener.
system IN: Message delivery system.
Returns:
HxResult: Returns HX_OK if successful.
